key_terms.meaning: Computer-controlled integration of two or more media types — text, graphics, images, audio, video, animation — into one presentation
The property that the user's input changes what the presentation shows or plays next; it separates multimedia from plain television
Hyperlinked multimedia: text, images, audio and video joined by links the user follows
The numeric value stored for one text character, e.g. 65 for 'A' in ASCII or a Unicode code point
One picture element; the smallest addressable dot of a raster image, storing one colour value
One measured value of a sound waveform, taken at the sampling rate, e.g. 44 100 samples per second
One complete still picture in a video sequence; the frame rate counts how many are shown per second
A graphic stored as a rectangular grid of pixels, so zooming magnifies the pixel squares
A graphic stored as drawing commands (lines, curves, fills) that are re-rendered at any size
The scheme that says how stored numbers map to colour, e.g. 24-bit RGB, 8-bit palette index, CMYK, grayscale
GIF (Graphics Interchange Format) uses LZW lossless compression, at most 256 palette colours, and supports simple frame animation
A lossy still-image format based on the DCT and coarse quantisation of high-frequency detail; good for photographs
A lossless raster format with per-pixel prediction filters and DEFLATE compression; supports true colour and alpha
Scalable Vector Graphics: an XML text file of drawing commands, resolution-independent and searchable as text
COder-DECoder: the algorithm that compresses a stream for storage and reconstructs it for playback
A file that wraps one or more compressed streams plus timing and metadata; the container is not the codec
Compression from which the exact original bytes can be rebuilt, e.g. PNG, FLAC, ZIP
Compression that throws away detail judged unimportant, so the output differs from the original, e.g. JPEG, MP3
A loud tone hides a quieter tone close to it in frequency or time, so those quiet components can be dropped without being heard
Video coding that predicts each block from a shifted region of an earlier frame and sends only the motion vector plus the residual
A standard for describing multimedia content (metadata) so it can be searched — not a compression standard
Keeping timed media at their intended relative times during capture, transmission and presentation

takeaways: Multimedia means several media types integrated under computer control, and interactivity is what makes it different from broadcast.
Every medium reduces to one digital unit: a character code, a pixel, a drawing command, an audio sample or a video frame.
A multimedia system is layers: capture and display hardware, operating-system drivers, codecs, and authoring or playback software on top.
A file format decides how pixels or drawing commands, colour information and metadata are laid out on disk, often with compression built in.
A container holds streams; a codec compresses each stream; the two are chosen independently (an MP4 file can carry H.264 video and AAC audio).
Compression works by removing redundancy: lossless methods rebuild exact data, lossy methods discard detail the eye or ear notices least.
Audio compression exploits frequency masking; video compression adds inter-frame prediction and motion compensation on top of intra-frame coding.
The MPEG family standardises how audio and video are compressed for interchange, while MPEG-7 standardises descriptions used for searching.
Synchronization must be maintained at capture, over the network and at playback, and drift is the error you must bound.
bank_note: Long answers here usually ask you to compare formats and codecs on concrete grounds (size, quality, transparency, animation, suitability for web) and to explain compression and synchronisation with a worked numeric example rather than a list.

bank.q: Define multimedia and list its elements. Explain why interactivity is treated as a defining feature rather than an optional extra.
outline: Definition: computer-controlled integration of text, graphics, images, audio, video and animation
Each element named with one example
Interactivity: user input alters the flow — hyperlinks, navigation, games, e-learning quizzes
Contrast with linear media such as cinema or broadcast TV
Applications: advertising, education, entertainment, medicine, public information, training

bank.q: Distinguish non-temporal from temporal media and give the digital unit and data-rate formula for each medium.
outline: Non-temporal: text, graphics, still images — no inherent time axis
Temporal: audio, video, animation — meaning depends on playback timing
Digital units: character code, pixel, vector command, audio sample, video frame
Audio rate = sampling rate × bits per sample × channels
Video rate = width × height × bits per pixel × frames per second
Why temporal media must be delivered at a steady rate

bank.q: Explain what an image file format must record, and compare BMP, JPEG and PNG on colour, compression and typical use.
outline: Header: dimensions, colour depth, colour mode, compression tag, metadata
Pixel data layout, row order and padding
BMP: uncompressed or simple RLE, large files, no loss
JPEG: DCT-based lossy, 24-bit colour, no alpha, photographs
PNG: lossless DEFLATE with prediction filters, true colour plus alpha, line art and web

bank.q: Explain the difference between a codec and a container, with two examples of each and one valid pairing.
outline: Codec = algorithm compressing and reconstructing one stream
Container = file structure holding streams, timing, metadata, index
Container examples: MP4, AVI, MKV, WebM; codec examples: H.264, HEVC, AAC, MP3, Opus
A file extension names the container, not the codec inside
Pairing example: .mp4 container with H.264 video and AAC audio
Consequence: a player may open the container but fail on an unsupported codec

bank.q: Explain lossless and lossy compression, state the principle each relies on, and give two formats of each kind.
outline: Compression removes redundancy: statistical, spatial, temporal, perceptual
Lossless: run-length, Huffman, LZW, DEFLATE; exact reconstruction; PNG, GIF, FLAC, ZIP
Lossy: quantisation and perceptual modelling; output differs; JPEG, MP3, H.264
Compression ratio definition: original size ÷ compressed size
Trade-off: ratio against quality and against compute cost

bank.q: A 30-second stereo music clip is recorded at 44.1 kHz with 16-bit samples. Compute the raw size, then the size when encoded as MP3 at 128 kbit/s, and state the compression ratio.
outline: Ratio ≈ 11 : 1
Comment: the saving is possible because masking hides most of the signal detail

bank.q: A video is 1920 × 1080 pixels, 24 bits per pixel, 25 frames per second. Compute the raw bit rate, then explain how inter-frame prediction and motion compensation reduce the stored rate.
outline: Bits per frame = 1920 × 1080 × 24 ≈ 49.8 Mbit
Raw rate ≈ 49.8 × 25 ≈ 1244 Mbit/s (about 1.24 Gbit/s)
Compression steps: colour subsampling, DCT and quantisation within a frame
Inter-frame prediction: send difference from a similar earlier frame
Motion compensation: send motion vector for a block plus small residual
Only residuals and vectors are coded, so the rate falls by orders of magnitude

bank.q: Draw the layered architecture of a multimedia system and place a capture card, a device driver, a codec, a media framework and an authoring tool in it.
outline: Layers from bottom: hardware, operating-system drivers, codecs and media framework, authoring and playback applications
Capture hardware: camera, microphone, frame grabber; output: display, speakers
Drivers give a uniform interface and hide device detail
Codecs supply compression and decompression; framework handles scheduling and synchronisation
Authoring software builds the presentation; the user interacts at the top layer
Note operating-system support for real-time scheduling and buffering

bank.q: A slide show must play a 20-second narration with a timed sequence of images and one video clip. Design a synchronisation scheme and explain how you detect and correct drift.
outline: Build a timeline with a common clock; give each media object a start time and duration
Use presentation time stamps on each unit and a buffer before playback
Choose a master clock (audio, since the ear notices gaps) and slave the rest
Measure drift = actual presentation time − intended time
Correct small drift by dropping or repeating frames; large drift by resynchronising at a cue point
Handle late data with a bounded buffer and a defined policy on underrun

bank.q: Compare GIF, PNG and JPEG for (a) a flat-colour company logo on a web page and (b) a photograph. Recommend a format for each and justify the choice.
outline: GIF: palette of at most 256 colours, LZW lossless, binary transparency, simple animation
PNG: true colour, full alpha, lossless but larger for photographs
JPEG: lossy, strong on photographs, visible ringing on sharp flat edges
Logo: PNG (or SVG if drawn as vectors) — sharp edges, alpha, no artefacts
Photograph: JPEG at a suitable quality setting for size
Note that repeated JPEG re-saving accumulates loss

bank.q: Evaluate lossy against lossless compression for two cases: archiving a hospital X-ray and streaming music to a phone on a metered connection.
outline: Lossless keeps exact values; lossy may discard diagnostic detail
X-ray: lossless because diagnosis depends on fine structure and legal record keeping
Streaming music: lossy is acceptable because masking hides removed components and bandwidth is limited
Cost argument in rupees per GB of mobile data
Decision rule: if a wrong pixel or sample changes the decision, use lossless
Mention that lossy artefacts compound on re-encoding

bank.q: Explain perceptual masking in audio coding and analyse how a psychoacoustic model decides what can be discarded.
outline: Transform or filterbank splits the signal into frequency bands
Threshold in quiet and masking threshold from loud components
Masked components below the threshold are not coded
Quantisation of remaining bands is set by the masking threshold (bit allocation)
Result: fewer bits for the same perceived quality
Limits: pre-echo on sharp transients, degradation at low bit rates

bank.q: Outline the MPEG family of standards and explain how MPEG-7 differs in purpose from MPEG-1, MPEG-2 and MPEG-4. Evaluate one use of MPEG-7 descriptions.
outline: MPEG-1: coding for CD-ROM video and audio layers
MPEG-2: broadcast-quality video and transport stream
MPEG-4: object-based coding, low bit rates, wider applications
MPEG-7: description of content — descriptors, description schemes, metadata, not compression
Use case: content-based retrieval of a video by colour, motion or spoken keyword
Evaluation: searching large archives, but descriptions must be created and standardised vocabularies limit free text
MPEG-21 as the later framework for delivery and rights

bank.q: Discuss synchronisation in multimedia presentations across capture, transmission and presentation, and evaluate the role of buffering, RTP time stamps and quality-of-service guarantees.
outline: Define the synchronisation requirement: intended relative timing of media units
Capture: common clock across camera and microphone; time stamps at source
Transmission: variable delay and jitter; RTP time stamps and sequence numbers; RTCP feedback
Presentation: buffer, master clock, playout schedule
QoS: reservation such as RSVP versus best-effort with adaptation
Evaluate: buffering adds latency but absorbs jitter; reservations cost network resources
Lip-sync tolerance figures and the effect of drift on the viewer

glossary.def: A computer-controlled presentation that combines two or more media types and lets the user interact with it.
The property that user input changes what the system presents next.
Multimedia content joined by links that the reader follows, as on a web page.
Media such as text, graphics and still images whose meaning does not depend on when they are shown.
Media such as audio, video and animation whose meaning depends on the timing of playback.
How many samples of a signal are taken per second, e.g. 44 100 Hz for CD audio.
Rounding each sample or coefficient to a limited set of levels, which introduces error and is the main lossy step.
The number of bits used to store the colour of one pixel, e.g. 24 bits for 8 bits each of red, green and blue.
A small table of selected colours where each pixel stores an index into the table instead of a full colour value.
Extra per-pixel data giving opacity, so an image can be composited over another.
Images stored as a grid of pixels, tied to a fixed resolution.
Images stored as geometric commands that are rendered at the current resolution.
A sequence of images shown in order so that objects appear to move or change.
The algorithm that compresses a media stream and reconstructs it for playback.
A file structure that carries compressed streams, timing information and metadata; it is not itself a codec.
The number of bits a stream carries per second, usually stated in kbit/s or Mbit/s.
Original data size divided by compressed data size, quoted as a ratio such as 11 : 1.
Compression after which the original data can be rebuilt exactly.
Compression that permanently discards detail to gain a much smaller file.
Compressing a frame using only its own pixels, as a still image is compressed.
Compressing a frame by predicting it from other frames in the sequence.
The displacement that points from a block in the current frame to the best matching region in a reference frame.
The ordered set of I, P and B frames between two independently decodable points in a video stream.
Delivering media so playback can begin before the whole file has arrived.
Variation in the delay of packets, which must be absorbed by a buffer before playback.
The growing difference between the intended and actual presentation time of a media unit.
